planting.note: Scatter seed on bare, well-drained soil in fall so it overwinters as a low rosette and opens its first white blooms in earliest spring.

directions: This tiny south-central US native forms low mounds of narrow leaves topped with small white, yellow-centered daisies that appear earlier than almost any other prairie wildflower. It thrives in lean, gravelly or chalky soils where richer plants struggle, and needs no supplemental feeding. Once established it self-sows readily along disturbed edges and rock outcrops, providing an early nectar source for small native bees before most other flowers have started. Let seed heads mature and shatter in place to keep a patch going year after year.

planting.note: Direct sow into disturbed, well-drained soil after the last frost; this rangeland annual germinates readily on bare ground and needs no coddling.

directions: Named for its habit of keeping its lemon-yellow ray flowers closed until around midday, this branching Texas and Oklahoma native colonizes disturbed prairie, roadsides, and stream banks with minimal care. It tolerates poor, dry sand or clay and largely shrugs off summer heat once seedlings are established. Leave some plants unpulled at season's end so seed can scatter and refresh the patch the following year. It is a reliable, low-input filler for a wildflower meadow mix rather than a formal border plant.

planting.note: Direct sow into lean, rocky or limestone-derived soil; this drought-tough Hill Country native resents rich, wet ground and needs excellent drainage to persist.

directions: A close cousin of soft greeneyes, Texas greeneyes carries cheerful yellow ray flowers around a papery green-and-maroon disk from early summer well into fall. It favors the drier, rockier limestone prairies and open woods of central and west Texas, where its deep taproot lets it shrug off drought once established. Give it a hot, sunny spot with sharp drainage and avoid overwatering, which shortens its lifespan. The long bloom season makes it a steady nectar source for native bees through the hottest months.

planting.note: Sow directly in fall so seedlings overwinter as a basal rosette and bloom the following summer, or sow in early spring for later-season flowers.

directions: This widespread eastern and central North American native produces airy sprays of small white, yellow-centered flowers over a long early- to late-summer season. It adapts readily to average garden soil, meadows, or disturbed edges and needs no fertilizer to perform well. Its abundant small flowers draw an unusually wide range of visitors, including sweat bees, hoverflies, and small butterflies, making it a workhorse in a naturalistic pollinator planting. Because it self-sows freely, site it where some spread is welcome or deadhead before seed set to keep it in bounds.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions into dry, rocky or caliche-rich soil in spring; this low prairie native spreads slowly by rhizome once established.

directions: Native to the prairies of Texas and Oklahoma, this low mounding perennial produces small lavender-blue tubular flowers over an extended bloom from spring through fall. It thrives in poor, rocky, or caliche soils where competition is low and rainfall is unreliable, needing almost no supplemental water once established. Its spreading habit makes it a useful groundcover for a hot, dry native bed, and its flowers draw a steady stream of small native bees and butterflies. Trim lightly after a flush of bloom to keep the mound tidy and encourage repeat flowering.
